summary.text: Lucas-type binomial congruences, together with pairing the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(k+p\), show that both sums vanish modulo \(p\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\); direct endpoint calculations give \(a(p-1)=1\) and \(c(p-1)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Thus each Hankel matrix is zero beyond its anti-diagonal, so only the reversal permutation contributes to its determinant; its sign is \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), which yields the first result and cancels the anti-diagonal factor in the second.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
       \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},
\]
so that \(p=2m+1\).
All congruences below are modulo \(p\), unless otherwise indicated.

We will prove two facts about each sequence:

1. its terms vanish modulo \(p\) throughout the interval
   \(p\le n\le 2p-2\);
2. its value at \(p-1\) can be evaluated explicitly.

These facts make both Hankel matrices anti-triangular modulo \(p\), after which their determinants are immediate.

We repeatedly use the following one-digit form of Lucas's congruence:
\[
\binom NK\equiv
\binom{N\bmod p}{K\bmod p}
\binom{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{\lfloor K/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
This is the usual Lucas congruence, and in the ranges used below it contains all the information we need. It follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\((1+x)^N\) after using
\((1+x)^p\equiv 1+x^p\pmod p\).
We also use the convention \(\binom uv=0\) when \(v>u\).

First observe that for every \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv \frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k.
\]
Division by \(k!\) is legitimate modulo \(p\), since \(k<p\).

We will also need a simple consequence of Lucas's congruence for central binomial coefficients. If
\[
m<q<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom{2q}{q}\equiv0.
\tag{3}
\]
In fact, \(p\le 2q<2p\), so the least base-\(p\) digit of \(2q\) is \(2q-p\), while that of \(q\) is \(q\). Since \(2q-p<q\), formula (1) contains the factor
\(\binom{2q-p}{q}=0\).

### 1. The special values at \(p-1\)

By (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(p=2m+1\) summands. Pairing the first \(2m\) of them as
\(1-1\), and retaining the final \(+1\), gives
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.
\tag{4}
\]

We next evaluate \(c(p-1)\). Its \(k\)-th summand is
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^2
\binom{2k}{k}
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}.
\tag{5}
\]
If \(k>m\), then \(k<p\) and (3) makes \(\binom{2k}{k}\) zero modulo \(p\). If \(k<m\), then
\(p-1-k>m\) and \(p-1-k<p\), so (3) instead makes the last central binomial coefficient zero. Thus every summand except the one with \(k=m\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

For \(k=m\), we have \(p-1-m=m\) and \(2m=p-1\). Consequently (2) gives
\[
\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m,
\qquad
\binom{2m}{m}=\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
The surviving summand is therefore
\[
(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^2(-1)^m(-1)^m
=(-1)^{5m}=(-1)^m.
\]
Hence
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.
\tag{6}
\]

### 2. Vanishing of \(a(n)\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\)

Let \(n\) lie in this interval and write
\[
n=p+r,
\qquad 0\le r\le p-2.
\]
Split the defining sum for \(a(n)\) into the three ranges
\[
0\le k\le r,
\qquad r<k<p,
\qquad p\le k\le p+r.
\]

For \(r<k<p\), Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}
\equiv \binom rk\binom10=0,
\tag{7}
\]
so every summand in the middle range vanishes.

The terms in the first and third ranges can be paired, pairing \(k\) with \(k+p\) for \(0\le k\le r\). Again by (1),
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}
\equiv \binom rk\binom10=\binom rk,
\tag{8}
\]
whereas
\[
\binom{p+r}{k+p}
\equiv \binom rk\binom11=\binom rk.
\tag{9}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{k+p}=-(-1)^k.
\tag{10}
\]
Therefore the two paired summands satisfy
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
+(-1)^{k+p}\binom{p+r}{k+p}^4\equiv0.
\]
All terms either vanish by (7) or cancel in one of these pairs. Thus
\[
a(n)\equiv0
\quad\text{for }p\le n\le2p-2.
\tag{11}
\]

### 3. Vanishing of \(c(n)\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\)

Let again \(n=p+r\), where \(0\le r\le p-2\). For brevity, write
\[
B(t)=\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
The \(k\)-th summand of \(c(n)\) is
\[
T_k=(-1)^k\binom nk^2 B(k)B(n-k).
\tag{12}
\]
As in (7), if \(r<k<p\), then \(\binom nk\equiv0\), so all terms in this middle interval vanish.

It remains to pair \(T_k\) with \(T_{k+p}\) for \(0\le k\le r\). Put
\[
s=r-k.
\]
Then
\[
n-k=p+s,
\qquad n-(k+p)=s.
\]
Equations (8) and (9) say
\[
\binom nk\equiv\binom n{k+p}\equiv\binom rk.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus, apart from the opposite signs supplied by (10), it remains to compare
\[
B(k)B(p+s)
\quad\text{and}\quad
B(k+p)B(s).
\tag{14}
\]
We do this by three exhaustive cases.

**First case: \(2k\ge p\).** Since \(k\le r<p\), this means \(m<k<p\), so (3) gives
\[
B(k)\equiv0.
\]
Also
\[
B(k+p)=\binom{2k+2p}{k+p}.
\]
Because \(p\le2k<2p\), the least base-\(p\) digits in this binomial coefficient are \(2k-p\) and \(k\), respectively. Since \(2k-p<k\), Lucas's congruence gives
\[
B(k+p)\equiv0.
\]
Thus both products in (14) vanish, and hence both terms in the pair vanish.

**Second case: \(2k<p\), but \(2s\ge p\).** The same argument, now applied to \(s<p\), gives
\[
B(s)\equiv0.
\]
Moreover
\[
B(p+s)=\binom{2s+2p}{s+p}\equiv0,
\]
because the least base-\(p\) digits are \(2s-p<s\) and \(s\). Again both products in (14), and therefore both terms in the pair, vanish.

**Third case: \(2k<p\) and \(2s<p\).** Lucas's congruence now gives precise nonzero relations. For the first shifted central binomial coefficient,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(k+p)
 &=\binom{2k+2p}{k+p}\\
 &\equiv \binom{2k}{k}\binom21
 =2B(k).
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
Likewise,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(p+s)
 &=\binom{2s+2p}{s+p}\\
 &\equiv \binom{2s}{s}\binom21
 =2B(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
It follows that
\[
B(k)B(p+s)\equiv 2B(k)B(s)
\equiv B(k+p)B(s).
\tag{17}
\]
By (13), the squared ordinary binomial factors in \(T_k\) and \(T_{k+p}\) are equal modulo \(p\); by (17), their products of central binomial coefficients are equal; and by (10), their signs are opposite. Hence
\[
T_k+T_{k+p}\equiv0.
\]

These three cases cover every \(0\le k\le r\). The middle interval \(r<k<p\) vanishes, and all remaining terms cancel in pairs. Therefore
\[
c(n)\equiv0
\quad\text{for }p\le n\le2p-2.
\tag{18}
\]

### 4. A determinant lemma for the anti-triangular shape

Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) be any \(p\times p\) matrix over a commutative ring, and suppose
\[
M_{ij}=0\qquad\text{whenever }i+j\ge p.
\tag{19}
\]
We claim that only the reversing permutation
\[
\rho(i)=p-1-i
\tag{20}
\]
can contribute a nonzero term to the Leibniz expansion of \(\det M\).

Indeed, consider a permutation \(\sigma\) for which every selected entry could be nonzero. Then
\[
i+\sigma(i)\le p-1
\qquad(0\le i<p).
\tag{21}
\]
Summing these inequalities gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\bigl(i+\sigma(i)\bigr)\le p(p-1).
\]
But \(\sigma\) merely permutes \(0,1,\dots,p-1\), so the left side equals
\[
2\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}i
=2\cdot\frac{p(p-1)}2
=p(p-1).
\]
Thus equality holds in the sum of (21). Since every summand is at most \(p-1\), every one must equal \(p-1\). Hence
\[
i+\sigma(i)=p-1
\]
for every \(i\), which forces \(\sigma=\rho\). Every other permutation selects at least one entry with row index plus column index at least \(p\), and its product is zero by (19).

Consequently,
\[
\det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{p-1-i,i}.
\tag{22}
\]
The reversing permutation reverses the order of every pair of distinct indices, so it has exactly
\(\binom p2=p(p-1)/2\) inversions. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\tag{23}
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm=(2m+1)m=2m^2+m,
\]
and hence
\[
(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=(-1)^m.
\tag{24}
\]

### 5. The determinant formed from \(a(n)\)

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
We work modulo \(p\). Since \(0\le i,j<p\), one always has
\[
i+j\le2p-2.
\]
If \(i+j\ge p\), equation (11) gives
\[
a(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus the reduction of \(A\) modulo \(p\) satisfies the anti-triangular hypothesis (19). Every entry on its anti-diagonal has index sum \(p-1\), and by (4) equals \(1\) modulo \(p\). Applying (22)--(24),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det A
&\equiv (-1)^{p(p-1)/2}
   \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}a(p-1)\\
&\equiv (-1)^m\cdot1^p\\
&=(-1)^m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Recalling \(m=(p-1)/2\), this is
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.}
\]

### 6. The determinant formed from \(c(n)\)

Let
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Equation (18) shows that its reduction modulo \(p\) also satisfies (19). Its anti-diagonal entries all equal \(c(p-1)\), which by (6) is \((-1)^m\). Therefore (22)--(24) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det C
&\equiv (-1)^{p(p-1)/2}
   \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}c(p-1)\\
&\equiv (-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd,
\[
\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^{mp}=(-1)^m.
\]
Hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^m(-1)^m=(-1)^{2m}=1.
\]
That is,
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.}
\]

Both asserted congruences follow.
